'''''Robin Hood''''' is a 2010 [[Historical fiction|historical]] [[action film]] directed by [[Ridley Scott]] and written by [[Brian Helgeland]], which was based on a story written by Helgeland and the writing duo of [[Ethan Reiff and Cyrus Voris]]. It stars [[Russell Crowe]] as the [[Robin Hood|outlaw legend]], alongside [[Cate Blanchett]], [[William Hurt]], [[Mark Strong]], [[Mark Addy]], [[Oscar Isaac]], [[Danny Huston]], [[Eileen Atkins]], and [[Max von Sydow]].

Development began on the project in January 2007 with [[Universal Pictures]]' purchase of a spec script by Reiff and Voris, which would see the film focus on a more prominent and sympathetic [[Sheriff of Nottingham]]. Casting Crowe in the title role, Ridley Scott was hired to direct later that same year. Rewrites delayed the film throughout 2008, with Helgeland hired to rewrite the screenplay, which saw a refocus of the story to be about Robin Hood once again, abandoning the Nottingham angle entirely. Filming commenced in March 2009 throughout [[England]] and [[Wales]].

''Robin Hood'' held its world premiere at the [[2010 Cannes Film Festival]] on 12 May 2010, the same day as its United Kingdom and Ireland release, and was later released on 14 May in the United States by Universal Pictures. The film received mixed reviews from critics and grossed $322 million worldwide against a $155–237 million budget.

==Plot==
{{Anchor|Premise}}
In AD 1199, Robin Longstride serves as a common [[archery|archer]] in the army of [[King Richard the Lionheart]]. A veteran of [[Third Crusade|Richard's crusade]], he now takes part in the siege of [[Château de Châlus-Chabrol|Chalus Castle]]. Disillusioned, war-weary, and facing charges of misconduct after a tavern brawl, he gives a frank but unflattering appraisal of the King's conduct when the King asks for it, and Robin and his comrades—archers [[Alan-a-Dale|Allan A'Dayle]] and [[Will Scarlett]] and soldier [[Little John]]—are locked in the [[stocks]].

After the King is killed during an attack on the castle, Robin and his comrades manage to free themselves and desert. They come across an ambush of the English royal guard by Godfrey, an English knight who has conspired with [[Philip II of France|King Philip of France]] to assassinate King Richard. After pursuing Godfrey away, Robin and his Merry Men take advantage of the situation by impersonating the dead English knights to return to England, as they fear they will not be able to afford the passage during the ensuing retreat. Before they depart to sail across the Channel, he promises a dying knight, Sir Robert of Loxley, to return his sword to his father in [[Nottingham]] and deliver the news of the King's death.

Awaking to find their ship arrived in the Thames estuary, Robin must continue to assume the identity of Loxley to deliver Richard's crown to the Royal Family. He witnesses the coronation of [[John, King of England|King John]], who orders the collection of harsh new taxes. [[William Marshal, 1st Earl of Pembroke|William Marshal]], the [[Lord Chancellor]] since the days of John's [[Henry II of England|father]], opposes the new taxes and is relieved of his position by John. The new king dispatches Godfrey to the [[Northern England|North]] to collect the taxes—unaware that Godfrey will instead use French troops to stir up unrest and prepare for King Philip to invade England. In secret, spies working for Marshal follow Godfrey's men and learn of the planned invasion of England.

Robin and his companions head to Nottingham, where Loxley's elderly and blind father, Sir Walter, asks him to continue impersonating his son to prevent the Crown from seizing the Loxley family lands. Loxley's widow, [[Maid Marian|Lady Marian]], is initially cold toward Robin, but warms to him when he and his men recover grain for the townsfolk to plant.

Godfrey's actions incite the northern barons, who march to meet King John. Speaking now for Sir Walter, Robin proposes that King John agree to a [[Magna Carta|charter of rights]] to ensure the rights of every Englishman and to unite his country. Realizing Godfrey's deception, and knowing he must meet the French invasion with an army, the King agrees. Meanwhile, French marauders plunder Nottingham. Robin and the northern barons arrive to stop Godfrey's men, but not before Godfrey has slain the blind Sir Walter.

As the main French expeditionary force begins its invasion of England on a beach below the [[White Cliffs of Dover|cliffs of Dover]], Robin leads the now united English army against them and Marian joins the fray with the forest orphans at her side. In the midst of the battle, Robin duels with Godfrey, who attempts to kill Marian and flees until Robin finally puts an arrow through his neck from afar. King Philip realizes that his plan to divide England has failed and calls off his invasion. When King John sees the French surrendering to Robin instead of to himself, he senses a threat to his power.

In London, King John reneges on his promise to sign the charter and declares Robin an [[outlaw]] to be hunted throughout the kingdom. The [[Sheriff of Nottingham]] announces the decree, and Robin and his men flee to [[Sherwood Forest]] with the orphans of Nottingham. Marian narrates their new life in the greenwood, noting that they live in equality as they right the many wrongs in the kingdom of King John.

==Production==
===Development and pre-production===
[[File:Louis John Rhead - The Sheriff Of Nottingham.jpg|thumb|left|upright|Earlier drafts of the script featured a bigger, more sympathetic focus on the [[Sheriff of Nottingham]], with one idea being Robin Hood beginning as the Sheriff.]]

In January 2007, [[Universal Pictures|Universal Studios]] and [[Brian Grazer]]'s [[Imagine Entertainment]] acquired a [[spec script]] written by Ethan Reiff and Cyrus Voris, creators of the television series ''[[Sleeper Cell (TV series)|Sleeper Cell]]''. Their script portrayed a more sympathetic [[Sheriff of Nottingham]] and less virtuous [[Robin Hood]], who becomes involved in a love triangle with [[Maid Marian|Lady Marian]]. The writers received a seven-figure deal for the purchase.<ref name=flies>{{cite journal | first=Michael | last=Fleming |author2=Diane Garrett | url=https://variety.com/2007/film/features/universal-flies-with-crowe-1117958414/ | title=Universal flies with Crowe | journal=Variety | date=31 January 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161230160300/https://variety.com/2007/film/features/universal-flies-with-crowe-1117958414/|archive-date=December 30, 2016| access-date=30 April 2007|url-status=live}}</ref> The following April, [[Ridley Scott]] was hired to direct the film, with [[Sam Raimi]] and [[Bryan Singer]] also considered for the position.<ref name=set>{{cite journal | first=Michael | last=Fleming | url=https://variety.com/2007/film/markets-festivals/scott-set-for-nottingham-1117963977/ | title=Scott set for 'Nottingham' | journal=Variety | date=29 April 2007 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160122015133/https://variety.com/2007/film/markets-festivals/scott-set-for-nottingham-1117963977/|archive-date=January 22, 2016|access-date=30 April 2007|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Sciretta |first1=Peter |title=Russell Crowe says Robin Hood was the Bad Guy |date=February 2007 |url=https://www.slashfilm.com/russell-crowe-says-robin-hood-was-the-bad-guy/ |publisher=[[Slashfilm]] |access-date=28 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160807194040/http://www.slashfilm.com/russell-crowe-says-robin-hood-was-the-bad-guy/ |archive-date=7 August 2016 |url-status=live }}</ref> Scott had attempted to get rights for himself and [[20th Century Fox]], but had previously collaborated with Grazer on ''[[American Gangster (film)|American Gangster]]'' and signed on as director rather than a producer.<ref name="romp"/> Scott claimed two previous film adaptations of Robin Hood: ''[[The Adventures of Robin Hood]]'' (1938) and ''[[Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves]]'' (1991) had failed to hit the target, saying "the best, frankly, was [[Mel Brooks]]'s ''[[Robin Hood: Men in Tights|Men in Tights]]'' (1993), because [[Cary Elwes]] was quite a comic".<ref name="cheese">{{cite news|date=9 November 2008|first= Garth|last=Pearce|title= Russell Crowe to toughen up Robin Hood|work=[[The Times]]|url=http://entertainment.timesonline.co.uk/tol/arts_and_entertainment/film/article5114486.ece|quote=I am trying to think of the last good one," said Scott. "Errol Flynn? A bit cheesy? A big cheese. God bless him. Kevin Costner? In the wig, you mean? The one I thought was the best, frankly, was Mel Brooks's Men in Tights, because Cary Elwes [who played Robin] was quite a comic. <!-- quote needed, link very likely to become unavailable -->| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090517082253/http://entertainment.timesonline.co.uk/tol/arts_and_entertainment/film/article5114486.ece|archive-date=17 May 2009|access-date=11 November 2008|url-status=dead|location=London}}{{subscription required}}</ref>

[[File:NASA Journey to Mars and “The Martian” (201508180030HQ).jpg|thumb|200px|Director Scott in 2015]]
Scott's dissatisfaction with the script led him to delay filming, and during 2008 it was rewritten into a story about Robin Hood becoming an outlaw; at one point Crowe was even being considered for a dual role as both Robin and the Sheriff. Scott dropped the latter notion and ''Nottingham'' was retitled to reflect the more traditional angle. In June, screenwriter [[Brian Helgeland]] was hired to rewrite the script by Reiff and Voris.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Kit |first1=Borys |title=Helgeland is new sheriff of 'Nottingham' |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/business/business-news/helgeland-is-new-sheriff-nottingham-137836/ |website=The Hollywood Reporter |access-date=29 March 2024 |date=5 June 2007}}</ref> Producer Marc Shmuger explained Scott had a different interpretation of the story from "the script, [which] had the sheriff of Nottingham as a ''[[CSI: Crime Scene Investigation|CSI]]''-style forensics investigator".<ref name="romp">{{cite news|first=Patrick|last=Goldstein|title='Nottingham': Will Russell Crowe ever romp in Sherwood Forest?|work=[[Los Angeles Times]]|date=7 August 2008|url=http://latimesblogs.latimes.com/the_big_picture/2008/08/nottingham-will.html|access-date=7 August 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080830100635/http://latimesblogs.latimes.com/the_big_picture/2008/08/nottingham-will.html|archive-date=30 August 2008|url-status=live}}</ref> Scott elaborated the script, portraying the Sheriff of Nottingham as being [[Richard I of England|Richard the Lionheart]]'s right-hand man, who returns to England to serve [[John, King of England|Prince John]] after Richard's assassination. Though Scott felt John "was actually pretty smart, he got a bad rap because he introduced taxation so he's the bad guy in this", and the Sheriff would have been torn between the "two wrongs" of a corrupt king and an outlaw inciting anarchy.<ref>{{cite news | first=Shawn | last=Adler | url=http://www.mtv.com/news/2429305/grazer-calls-scotts-nottingham-the-gladiator-of-robin-hood-movies/ | title=Grazer Calls Scott's 'Nottingham' The 'Gladiator' of Robin Hood Movies | work=MTV Movies Blog | date=22 October 2007 | access-date=29 April 2008 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080420081544/http://moviesblog.mtv.com/2007/10/22/grazer-calls-scotts-nottingham-the-gladiator-of-robin-hood-movies/ | archive-date=20 April 2008 | url-status=dead }}</ref> Locations were sought in North East England including [[Alnwick Castle]], [[Bamburgh Castle]] and [[Kielder Forest]]. A portion of filming was intended to take place in [[Northumberland]]. As a result of the [[2007–08 Writers Guild of America strike|WGA strike]], production was put on hold.<ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Lewinski |first1=John Scott |title=Nottingham Not in Cards for Ridley Scott, Russell Crowe |url=https://www.wired.com/2008/07/nottingham-not/ |magazine=[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]] |access-date=20 November 2020}}</ref>

Filming was scheduled to begin in August in [[Sherwood Forest]] if the [[2008 Screen Actors Guild strike]] did not take place,<ref>{{cite news | first = Claudia | last = Eller | author2 = Richard Verrier | title = Suspense scene | work = [[Los Angeles Times]] | date = 24 June 2008 | url = https://www.latimes.com/business/la-fi-actor24-2008jun24,0,4147025.story | access-date = 24 June 2008 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080627103526/http://www.latimes.com/business/la-fi-actor24-2008jun24,0,4147025.story | archive-date = 27 June 2008 | url-status = live }}</ref> for release on 26 November 2009. By July, filming was delayed,<ref>{{cite journal | first=Gregg | last=Kilday | url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/hr/content_display/film/news/e3if7b717939831cbe23d5f5d7875615784 | title=Ridley Scott's 'Nottingham' hits delay | journal=[[The Hollywood Reporter]] | date=27 July 2008 | access-date=26 July 2008 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080727135443/http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/hr/content_display/film/news/e3if7b717939831cbe23d5f5d7875615784 <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archive-date = 27 July 2008}}</ref> and playwright Paul Webb was hired to rewrite the script.<ref name="romp"/> The film was moved to 2010.<ref>{{cite journal|first=Pamela|last=McClintock|title='Wolfman,' 'Nottingham' delayed|journal=Variety|date=10 December 2008|url=https://variety.com/2008/film/markets-festivals/wolfman-nottingham-delayed-1117997153/ |access-date=10 December 2008}}</ref> The Sheriff of Nottingham's character was then merged with Robin.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Horowitz |first1=Josh |author-link=Josh Horowitz |title=BREAKING: Russell Crowe Will Play Robin Hood AND The Sheriff In Ridley Scott's 'Nottingham' |url=https://www.mtv.com/news/6j6ifi/breaking-russell-crowe-will-play-robin-hood-and-the-sheriff-in-ridley-scotts-nottingham |archive-date=29 March 2024 |website=MTV |access-date=29 March 2024 |language=en |date=27 September 2008}}</ref> Scott describes the identity of Robin, "In the context of the story he starts off as Helgeland returned to rewrite, adding an opening where Robin witnesses the Sheriff dying in battle, and takes over his identity.<ref name="confusion">{{cite web |last1=Horowitz |first1=Josh |title=Brian Grazer Reveals 'Nottingham' Plot Points, Sets Record Straight On Russell Crowe Confusion many trees which had not been [[pollarding|pollarded]].<ref name="cheese"/> By February 2009, Scott revealed ''Nottingham'' had become his version of ''Robin Hood'', as he had become dissatisfied with ===Casting===
[[Russell Crowe]] was cast into the role of Robin Hood in January 2007, with a fee of $20&nbsp;million against 20% of the gross.<ref name=flies/> The next addition to the cast was [[Mark Strong]]. When interviewed about his role, Strong stated his character of Sir Godfrey was originally called Conrad and was based on [[Guy of Gisbourne]]. He described the original character as having blond hair and being disfigured from being struck by a crossbow bolt.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Reynolds |first1=Simon |title=Strong joins Ridley Scott's 'Nottingham' |date=10 November 2008 |url=https://www.digitalspy.com/movies/a135178/strong-joins-ridley-scotts-nottingham/ |publisher=[[Digital Spy]] |access-date=17 April 2020 |archive-date=24 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201224235026/https://www.digitalspy.com/movies/a135178/strong-joins-ridley-scotts-nottingham/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090414080023/http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/hr/content_display/news/e3iddc0608768893d1e82e7cae7eec09ccd |archive-date=14 April 2009 }}</ref><ref>{{cite ===Filming===
[[File:Bourne Wood Movie Castle.jpg|thumb|right|350px|Mock castle at the Bourne Wood at the end of filming, showing the burnt-out castle gate]]
Filming began on 30 March 2009.<ref name="pressrelease">{{cite news|title=Ridley Scott's Robin Hood film begins production|work=In Contention|format=Press release|date=24 March 2009|url=http://www.incontention.com/?p=4917|access-date=24 March 2009}}</ref> In June and July, the crew filmed at [[Freshwater West]] beach, in [[Pembrokeshire]], Wales.<ref>{{cite news|title=Extras queue for Robin Hood roles|publisher=[[BBC News]]|date=9 May 2009|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/wales/8041103.stm|access-date=10 May 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090511071626/http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/wales/8041103.stm|archive-date=11 May 2009|url-status=live}}</ref> The arrival of the dead king's cog (boat), accompanied by Robin and his men, at the Tower of London was filmed at Virginia Water, where a partial mock-up of the Tower was built. Extensive scenes from the film were filmed on the [[Ashridge Estate]], [[Little Gaddesden]], on the [[Hertfordshire]]/[[Buckinghamshire]] border.<ref>{{cite news|title=How the National Trust came to the aid of Robin Hood |publisher=[[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] |date=9 May 2009 |url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-global/w-news/w-latest_news/w-news-how-the-national-trust-came-to-the-aid-of-robin-hood.htm |access-date=10 May 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100222033551/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-global/w-news/w-latest_news/w-news-how-the-national-trust-came-to-the-aid-of-robin-hood.htm |archive-date=22 February 2010 }}</ref> Filming of the siege of [[Château de Châlus-Chabrol|Castle Chalus]] took place at the [[Bourne Wood]] at [[Farnham]], Surrey during July and August.<ref name=SurreyLife>{{cite web | title=Surrey Film Locations | url=http://surrey.greatbritishlife.co.uk/article/surrey-film-locations-2505/ | work=Surrey Life | access-date=1 June 2010 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101226070622/http://surrey.greatbritishlife.co.uk/article/surrey-film-locations-2505/ | archive-date=26 December 2010 | df=dmy-all }}</ref> Filming also took place at [[Dovedale]] near [[Ashbourne, Derbyshire]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Russell Crowe in Ashbourne|publisher=BBC Derby|date=5 August 2009|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/derby/content/articles/2009/08/05/russell_crowe_in_ashbourne_2009_feature.shtml|access-date=5 August 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924205314/http://www.bbc.co.uk/derby/content/articles/2009/08/05/russell_crowe_in_ashbourne_2009_feature.shtml|archive-date=24 September 2015|url-status=live}}</ref> On July 31, thieves broke into the props building at night and stole cameras that were being used for the film.<ref>{{cite web |title=Robin Hood cameras stolen from studio |date=3 August 2009 |url=https://www.hollywood.com/celebrities/robin-hood-cameras-stolen-from-studio-57206929/ |publisher=[[Hollywood.com]] |access-date=17 April 2020 |archive-date=24 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201224235010/https://www.hollywood.com/celebrities/robin-hood-cameras-stolen-from-studio-57206929/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

The [[battering ram]] used during the filming at the Bourne Wood in Surrey, which was nicknamed 'Rosie' by the film crew and is worth [[Pound sterling|£]]60,000, was donated by Russell Crowe to a [[Scotland|Scottish]] charity, the [[The Clanranald Trust for Scotland|Clanranald Trust]] to be used for battle re-enactments at a fort named [[Duncarron]], built in a forest in [[North Lanarkshire]] near the [[Carron Valley Reservoir]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Charlie|first=Allan|title=Russell Crowe Helps a friend with a cause|url=http://www.clanranald.org/cln1/the-news/31-duncarron-news/111-russell-crowe-helps-a-friend-with-a-cause|publisher=The Clanranald Trust website|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131019154730/http://www.clanranald.org/cln1/the-news/31-duncarron-news/111-russell-crowe-helps-a-friend-with-a-cause|archive-date=19 October 2013}}</ref>

Crowe rode the same horse, George, that he had ridden in ''[[Gladiator (2000 film)|Gladiator]]''.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Longmire |first1=Becca |title=Russell Crowe Talks Reuniting With His 'Gladiator' Horse, Admits He Spoke To Him About Winning An Oscar |date=21 June 2019 |url=https://etcanada.com/news/466833/russell-crowe-talks-reuniting-with-his-gladiator-horse-admits-he-spoke-to-him-about-winning-an-oscar/#:~:text=Russell%20Crowe%20spoke%20about%20the,2010%20film%20%E2%80%9CRobin%20Hood%E2%80%9D. |publisher=[[Entertainment Tonight Canada]] |access-date=28 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200527092044/https://etcanada.com/news/466833/russell-crowe-talks-reuniting-with-his-gladiator-horse-admits-he-spoke-to-him-about-winning-an-oscar/#:~:text=Russell%20Crowe%20spoke%20about%20the,2010%20film%20%E2%80%9CRobin%20Hood%E2%80%9D. |archive-date=27 May 2020 |url-status=dead }}</ref> During the shoot, Crowe fractured both of his legs doing a scene in which he "jumped off a castle portcullis onto rock-hard uneven ground" and said he "never discussed the injury with production, never took a day off because of it, I just kept going to work", only learning about the injury from an [[Projectional radiography|X-ray]] a decade later.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://people.com/russell-crowe-reveals-fractured-both-legs-during-robin-hood-shoot-just-kept-going-exclusive-8584385|title=Russell Crowe Reveals He Fractured Both Legs During ''Robin Hood'' Shoot: 'I Just Kept Going' (Exclusive)|date=February 17, 2024|access-date=February 17, 2024|website=[[People (magazine)|People]]}}</ref>

===Visual effects===
[[Moving Picture Company]] (MPC) provided the visual effects for the film. Richard Stammers, MPC's visual effects supervisor, worked with Universal Pictures's visual effects producer Allen Maris to "achieve a wide range of visual effects", which included computer-animated armies, boats, arrows, and digital environments.<ref name="MPC">{{Cite web |title=''Robin Hood'' |url=https://www.mpcvfx.com/en/filmography/robin-hood/ |website=[[Moving Picture Company]] |access-date=6 December 2025}}</ref> A challenge for MPC was to create the invading French Armada and the ensuing battle with the English army; 200 computer-animated ships and 6000 soldiers were added to the 8 practical boats, with 500 extras used in principal photography. Alice, MPC's proprietary crowd generation software, was used to simulate the rowing and disembarkation of French soldiers and horses. The water interactions were generated using Flowline.<ref name="MPC"/> Matte paintings and computer-animated projections were used to reconstruct the medieval city in the film. MPC created cliffs to surround the beach environment, which was added to 75 shots.<ref name="MPC"/>

==Soundtrack==
{{Main|Robin Hood (2010 soundtrack)}}
The soundtrack to ''Robin Hood'', with music written and performed by [[Marc Streitenfeld]], was released on 11 May 2010.<ref>{{cite web |title=Robin Hood [2010] [Original Motion Picture Soundtrack] |url=https://www.allmusic.com/album/robin-hood-2010-original-motion-picture-soundtrack-mw0001981004 |publisher=[[AllMusic]] |access-date=28 July 2020 |archive-date=24 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201224235016/https://www.allmusic.com/album/robin-hood-2010-original-motion-picture-soundtrack-mw0001981004 |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Release==
''Robin Hood'' held its world premiere at the [[2010 Cannes Film Festival]] the same day as its [[United Kingdom]] and [[Republic of Ireland|Ireland]] releases. It was then released on 14 May 2010 in [[North America]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Leffler |first1=Rebecca |title='Robin Hood' to open Cannes |date=25 March 2010 |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/robin-hood-open-cannes-22043 |publisher=[[The Hollywood Reporter]] |access-date=28 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150806141857/http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/robin-hood-open-cannes-22043 |archive-date=6 August 2015 |url-status=live }}</ref> The film premiered in [[Japan]] on 10 December 2010.<ref name="japan-site">{{cite news |url=http://www.robinhood-movie.jp/ |title=ロビン・フッド公式サイト |access-date=20 May 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100523183106/http://www.robinhood-movie.jp/ |archive-date=23 May 2010 |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Home media===
''Robin Hood'' was released on [[DVD-Video|DVD]] and [[Blu-ray Disc]] on 20 September 2010 in the UK,<ref>[https://www.amazon.co.uk/Robin-Hood-Extended-Directors-Cut/dp/B003DZ131Y/ref=sr_1_2?s=dvd&ie=UTF8&qid=1359860713&sr=1-2 Amazon UK: ''Robin Hood – Extended Director's Cut (DVD)''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201224235015/https://www.amazon.co.uk/Robin-Hood-Extended-Directors-Cut/dp/B003DZ131Y/ref=sr_1_2?s=dvd&ie=UTF8&qid=1359860713&sr=1-2 |date=24 December 2020 }}. Retrieved 3 February 2013</ref> and the following day in the US.<ref>[https://www.amazon.com/Robin-Hood-Single-Disc-Unrated-Directors/dp/B003U0AHBO/ref=sr_1_6?s=movies-tv&ie=UTF8&qid=1359860487&sr=1-6&keywords=robin+hood Amazon US: ''Robin Hood (Single-Disc Unrated Director's Cut) (2010)''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201224235016/https://www.amazon.com/Robin-Hood-Single-Disc-Unrated-Directors/dp/B003U0AHBO/ref=sr_1_6?s=movies-tv&ie=UTF8&qid=1359860487&sr=1-6&keywords=robin+hood |date=24 December 2020 }}. Retrieved 3 February 2013</ref> While the UK home media releases only consisted of the extended 'Director's Cut' version (16 additional minutes), the US DVD and Blu-ray Discs consisted of both the 'Director's Cut' version and the shorter theatrical version.<ref>{{cite web|last=Kauffman|first=Jeffrey|title=Robin Hood Blu-ray|url=http://www.blu-ray.com/movies/Robin-Hood-Blu-ray/12967/#Review|publisher=Blu-ray.com|access-date=1 October 2012|date=15 September 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120831140820/http://www.blu-ray.com/movies/Robin-Hood-Blu-ray/12967/#Review|archive-date=31 August 2012|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Reception==

===Box office===
On its opening week, the film took in £5,750,332 in the UK, ahead of ''[[Iron Man 2]]'', and $36,063,385 in the US and Canada.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.screenrush.co.uk/films/film-126127/box-office/ |title=Box-Office for the film (Robin Hood) |work=Screenrush |access-date=10 October 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120310114850/http://www.screenrush.co.uk/films/film-126127/box-office/ |archive-date=10 March 2012 |url-status=live }}</ref> It grossed a total of £15,381,416 in the UK, $105.2 million in North America and $321,669,741 worldwide.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.boxofficemojo.com/movies/?id=nottingham.htm |title=Robin Hood (2010) |work=Box Office Mojo |date=5 August 2010 |access-date=10 October 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190609073345/https://www.boxofficemojo.com/movies/?id=nottingham.htm |archive-date=9 June 2019 |url-status=live }}</ref>
Although the film performed better overseas, the box office figures were still seen as somewhat of a disappointment. Brandon Gray of ''Box Office Mojo'' thought the take was unfairly maligned. Gray wrote that the film was among the highest grossing medieval-period films of all time, and that the true financial issue was the production going over budget rather than returns being particularly beneath expectations.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://boxofficemojo.com/news/?id=3051&p=.htm |title='Gulliver,' 'Persia,' 'Narnia' Rank Among the Big Botches of 2010 |work=Box Office Mojo |date=20 January 2011 |access-date=10 October 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111026085223/http://www.boxofficemojo.com/news/?id=3051&p=.htm |archive-date=26 October 2011 |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Critical reception===
{{Anchor|Critics}}
[[File:Russell Crowe.jpg|thumb|left|170px|Russell Crowe's performance as Robin earned a mixed response, with some specific criticism focused particularly on his accent in the film.]]
On review aggregate website [[Rotten Tomatoes]] the film holds an approval rating of 43% based on 251 reviews, with an average rating of 5.4/10. The website's critical consensus reads, "Ridley Scott's revisionist take on this oft-told tale offers some fine acting and a few gripping action sequences, but it's missing the thrill of adventure that made Robin Hood a legend in the first place."<ref name="tomatoes">{{cite Rotten Tomatoes | id = robin_hood_2010 | type = m | title = Robin Hood (2010) | access-date = 16 January 2021 | url = https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/robin_hood_2010/ | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20190523213128/https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/robin_hood_2010/ | archive-date = 23 May 2019 | url-status = dead }}</ref> [[Metacritic]] assigned the film a weighted average score of 53 out of 100, based on 40 critics, indicating "mixed or average reviews".<ref name="meta">{{cite Metacritic | id = robinhood2010 | type = movie | title = Robin Hood (2010) | access-date = 16 January 2021 | url = http://www.metacritic.com/film/titles/robinhood2010 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20100504150044/http://www.metacritic.com/film/titles/robinhood2010 | archive-date = 4 May 2010 | url-status = dead }}</ref> Audiences polled by [[CinemaScore]] gave the film an average grade of "B−" on an A+ to F scale.<ref name="CinemaScore">{{Cite web |url=http://www.cinemascore.com/ |title=CinemaScore |publisher=[[CinemaScore]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190809062201/http://cinemascore.com/publicsearch/index/title/ |archive-date=August 9, 2019 |access-date=December 14, 2020}}{{cbignore}} Each film's score can be accessed from the website's search bar.</ref>

[[Roger Ebert]] of the ''[[Chicago Sun-Times]]'' gave the film two stars out of four, writing that "little by little, title by title, innocence and joy is being drained out of the movies."<ref name="ebert">{{cite news|first=Roger|last=Ebert|author-link=Roger Ebert|title=Merry Men N The Hood|newspaper=[[Chicago Sun-Times]]|publisher=[[Sun-Times Media Group]]|location=Chicago, Illinois|url=https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/robin-hood-2010|date=12 May 2010|via=rogerebert.com|access-date=10 April 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100515103944/http://rogerebert.suntimes.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=%2F20100512%2FREVIEWS%2F100519992|archive-date=15 May 2010|url-status=dead}} {{Rating|2|4}}</ref> Joe Neumaier of the ''[[New York Daily News]]'' felt that "the problem with Russell Crowe's new take on the legend is that it has one muddy boot in history and the other in fantasy. The middling result is far from a bull's-eye."<ref>{{cite news| date = 11 May 2010| first = Joe| last = Naumier| title = Robin Hood| url = http://www.nydailynews.com/entertainment/movies/2010/05/11/2010-05-11_robin_hood_arrow_isnt_on_the_mark.html| work = [[New York Daily News]]| publisher = [[Tribune Publishing]]| location = New York City| access-date = 13 May 2010| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20100514154237/http://www.nydailynews.com/entertainment/movies/2010/05/11/2010-05-11_robin_hood_arrow_isnt_on_the_mark.html| archive-date = 14 May 2010| url-status = live}} {{Rating|3|5}}</ref> David Roark of ''[[Relevant (magazine)|Relevant]]'' accused Scott of replacing depth with detail and manipulative themes, like vengeance and unjust war, and stated that Scott had sucked the life out of a cherished fable, writing that "Scott has turned a myth, a concept essentially, into a history which emerges as dry, insensible clutter."<ref name="Relevant Magazine">{{cite web|first=David|last=Roark|url=http://www.relevantmagazine.com/culture/film/reviews/21555-robin-hood|title=Robin Hood—Review|work=[[Relevant (magazine)|Relevant]]|publisher=Relevant Media|location=Winter Park, Florida|access-date=7 July 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100519163010/http://www.relevantmagazine.com/culture/film/reviews/21555-robin-hood|archive-date=19 May 2010|url-status=dead}}</ref> [[Anthony Lane]], writing for ''[[The New Yorker]]'', found the film "dour and dun", and was critical of Crowe's performance, stating "His Robin, however, seems pathologically glum; even when leading a cavalry charge on a white steed, he cuts a lonesome figure, marooned in his own feuds and ruminations".<ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Lane |first1=Anthony |title=Straight Arrows |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2010/05/24/straight-arrows |magazine=[[The New Yorker]] |date=17 May 2010 |access-date=28 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190409195506/https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2010/05/24/straight-arrows |archive-date=9 April 2019 |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Owen Gleiberman]] of ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]'' was critical of the film not holding any traits of the Robin Hood myth, and said of Scott's direction and Crowe's performance "Scott and Crowe made a great movie out of ''Gladiator'', tapping deep into the showbiz masculine bravura of ancient-world Hollywood spectaculars. In Robin Hood, Scott tries to go deep again, but in a misguided way—he thinks he's making a pop-medieval ''[[Saving Private Ryan|Saving Private Robin]]''. The battles are grainy and "existential," but what they aren't is thrilling. They're surging crowd scenes with streams of arrows and flecks of blood, and Crowe, slashing his way through them, is a glorified extra. He's so grimly possessed with purpose that he's a bore, and so is the movie."<ref>{{cite web |last1=Gleiberman |first1=Owen |title=Robin Hood |url=https://ew.com/article/2010/05/17/robin-hood-4/ |publisher=[[Entertainment Weekly]] |access-date=28 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180222073746/http://ew.com/article/2010/05/17/robin-hood-4/ |archive-date=22 February 2018 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Among the film's more positive reviews, [[Mick LaSalle]] of the ''[[San Francisco Chronicle]]'' wrote that "Scott has great command of his action sequences" and praised his "sophisticated approach to the material."<ref>{{cite news|first=Mick|last=LaSalle|author-link=Mick LaSalle|url=http://www.sfgate.com/movies/article/Review-Gritty-variation-on-Robin-Hood-3188972.php|title=Review: Gritty variation on 'Robin Hood'|newspaper=[[San Francisco Chronicle]]|publisher=[[Hearst Communications|Hearst]]|location=San Francisco, California|date=14 May 2010|access-date=11 June 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131202231828/http://www.sfgate.com/movies/article/Review-Gritty-variation-on-Robin-Hood-3188972.php|archive-date=2 December 2013|url-status=live}}</ref> [[Ty Burr]] of ''[[The Boston Globe]]'' called the film "smart, muscular entertainment" and wrote that Crowe "possesses a presence and authority to make you forget all about [[Kevin Costner]]."<ref>[https://archive.boston.com/ae/movies/articles/2010/05/14/merry_men_with_muscle_in_robin_hood/ Robin Hood]  Ty Burr, ''The Boston Globe'', 14 May 2010</ref> Though he noted that the film downplayed several characters, Kirk Honeycutt of ''[[The Hollywood Reporter]]'' was complimentary of the film, praising [[John Mathieson (cinematographer)|John Mathieson]]'s cinematography and [[Marc Streitenfeld]]'s musical score.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Honeycutt |first1=Kirk |title='Robin Hood': Film Review |date=14 October 2010 |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/review/robin-hood-film-review-29565 |publisher=[[The Hollywood Reporter]] |access-date=28 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160810092501/http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/review/robin-hood-film-review-29565 |archive-date=10 August 2016 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Russell Crowe received criticism from the British media for his variable accent during the film. ''[[Empire (film magazine)|Empire]]'' said his accent was occasionally Scottish,<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.empireonline.com/reviews/reviewcomplete.asp?FID=134778 | first = Dan | last = Jolin | work = Empire | title = Reviews: Robin Hood | access-date = 14 May 2010 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120122104557/http://www.empireonline.com/reviews/reviewcomplete.asp?FID=134778 | archive-date = 22 January 2012 | url-status = live }}</ref> while ''[[Total Film]]'' thought there were also times when it sounded Irish.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.totalfilm.com/reviews/cinema/robin-hood-1 | author=Andy Lowe | work=Total Film Magazine | title=Reviews: Robin Hood | access-date=14 May 2010 | archive-date=24 December 2020 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201224235017/https://www.gamesradar.com/totalfilm/ | url-status=live }}</ref> [[Mark Lawson]], while interviewing Crowe on [[BBC Radio 4]], suggested there were hints of Irish in his accent, which angered Crowe who described this as "bollocks" and stormed out.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/organgrinder/2010/may/14/russell-crowe-accent-acrimony | author=John Plunkett | work=The Guardian (blog) | title=Russell Crowe puts accent on acrimony | date=14 May 2010 | access-date=14 May 2010 | location=London | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131204070218/http://www.theguardian.com/media/organgrinder/2010/may/14/russell-crowe-accent-acrimony | archive-date=4 December 2013 | url-status=live }} (Includes audio file)</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b00s8zd0 |title=Russell Crowe, Ashes to Ashes and the Archbishop of Canterbury |access-date=25 December 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190612204716/https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b00s8zd0 |archive-date=12 June 2019 |url-status=live }}</ref>

A number of reviewers have criticised historical inaccuracies in the film. In ''[[The New York Times]]'', [[A. O. Scott]] complained that the film made "a hash of the historical record".<ref>{{Cite web | last=Scott | first=A. O. | author-link=A. O. Scott | title=Rob the Rich? Give to the Poor? Oh, Puh-leeze! | url=https://movies.nytimes.com/2010/05/14/movies/14robin.html | work=[[The New York Times]] | date=13 May 2010 | access-date=15 July 2012 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120630203425/http://movies.nytimes.com/2010/05/14/movies/14robin.html | archive-date=30 June 2012 | url-status=live }}</ref> In ''[[The Guardian]]'', [[Alex von Tunzelmann]] complained that the film was filled with historical impossibilities and anachronisms. She notes that Richard the Lionheart was indeed fighting in France in 1199, but that he had actually come back from the Holy Land seven years earlier, so it is inaccurate to depict him fighting in France on his way back from the Holy Land in 1199, as is the case in the film.<ref>{{Cite web | last=Von Tunzelmann | first=Alex | author-link=Alex von Tunzelmann | title=Reel history special: Ridley Scott's Robin Hood – wide of the mark? | url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2010/sep/23/ridley-scott-robin-hood-russell-crowe | work=The Guardian | date=23 September 2010 | access-date=26 July 2012 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131204004412/http://www.theguardian.com/film/2010/sep/23/ridley-scott-robin-hood-russell-crowe | archive-date=4 December 2013 | url-status=live }}</ref>

==Potential sequels==
{{see also | Ridley Scott's unrealised projects#Robin Hood sequels }}
Scott indicated he had been considering a further film in an interview with ''[[The Times]]'' in April 2010, stating, "Let's say we might presume there's a sequel. [...] Honestly, I thought, 'Why not have the potential for a sequel, particularly if it is a genre that you absolutely love and has never been fully explored?' If there were to be a sequel, you would have a constant enemy throughout, King John, and you would follow his reign of 17 years. The signing of [[Magna Carta]] could be Robin's final act."<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radio/article/robin-to-the-maximus-fdl3btkpf7k | location=London | work=The Times | first=Will | last=Lawrence | title=Robin to the max(imus) | date=5 April 2010 | access-date=17 March 2026 }} {{subscription required}}</ref> In May 2010, while Scott was recovering from a knee operation, Crowe said "There's no sort of cynicism with this, we don't have two other scripts under Ridley's hospital bed [...] Obviously there's a figure in the studio heads' mind, if we pass a certain figure then they'll give us a call and say, 'well, tell the second part of the story', but there's no grand plan in that regard. [...] if I had the opportunity to address what happens next with Ridley and Cate, then great, let's do it."<ref>{{cite news| url=http://uk.reuters.com/article/idUKTRE64A6N620100513?pageNumber=1 | work=Reuters | title="Robin Hood" opens Cannes, Crowe hints at sequel | date=13 May 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200417211357/https://uk.reuters.com/article/uk-cannes/robin-hood-opens-cannes-crowe-hints-at-sequel-idUKTRE64A6N620100513?pageNumber=1 | archive-date=17 April 2020}}</ref>

In February 2026, Crowe looked back at the plans for sequels, saying that at the time the story was meant "To be told in three parts [...] When I started digging in to RH, I found the story and its roots in Greene Man mythology deeply interesting. The tale of Robin lasted hundreds of years, how? It was my idea to show that RH was a title, passed down, not one man."<ref>{{cite web | first=Wesley | last=Yin-Poole | title='The Director's Cut Is the Movie We All Thought We Were Releasing' — Russell Crowe Responds to Robin Hood's 'Unfair' Comparisons to Gladiator, 16 Years Later | date=16 February 2026 | website=[[IGN]] | url=https://www.ign.com/articles/the-directors-cut-is-the-movie-we-all-thought-we-were-releasing-russell-crowe-responds-to-robin-hoods-unfair-comparisons-to-gladiator-16-years-later | access-date=2026-03-17 }}</ref>
